definition: Biodiesel is an alternative diesel-engine fuel made by removing glycerin from vegetable oils; it contains no petroleum, generally runs in unmodified diesel engines, and is commonly blended with petroleum diesel in ratios denoted "Bxx" (percent biodiesel by volume).
core_idea: Biodiesel offers environmental and safety benefits over conventional diesel but suffers a fuel-economy penalty and, most importantly, remains substantially more expensive and limited in production volume.
key_points: Biodiesel is produced by removing glycerin from vegetable oils and contains no petroleum
Most diesel engines can run biodiesel without modification
Blend labeling convention: "Bxx" where xx is the percent biodiesel by volume (e.g., B20 = 20% biodiesel)
Advantages: biodegradable, renewable, generally lower emissions than standard diesel, nontoxic, higher flashpoint making it safer to transport and store
Disadvantages: about a 10% reduction in fuel economy and power versus diesel, acts as a stronger solvent than diesel, very high biodiesel percentages may require special engines
The biggest limitation is cost: biodiesel can currently only be produced in limited amounts and is substantially more expensive than regular diesel
